references.text: God sent his servants (the prophets) repeatedly to the people, but they were mocked and mistreated – the same pattern as in the parable where the vineyard workers abuse the master’s servants. [ref:2 Chr 36:15-16|2 Chronicles 36:15-16]

The Lord sent his servants, the prophets, again and again to Israel, but the people would not listen – paralleling how the owner of the vineyard sent servants who were rejected. [ref:Jer 7:25-26|Jeremiah 7:25-26]

The Lord sent his prophets early and late, but the people did not hear or turn back. The same theme appears where the vineyard owner sends servants who are rejected and mistreated. [ref:Jer 25:4-7|Jeremiah 25:4-7]
Matthew’s parallel account of the parable of the wicked tenants, in which the owner sends servants who are beaten, killed, and stoned. [ref:Matt 21:34-36|Matthew 21:34-36]
Mark’s parallel account where the vineyard owner sends several servants who are beaten and dishonored by the tenants. [ref:Mark 12:2-5|Mark 12:2-5]

Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, in which the Lord expected fruit but received wild grapes – the background for Jesus’ parable about the vineyard and the expectation to share in the harvest. [ref:Isa 5:1-4|Isaiah 5:1-4]
The people were stubborn and killed the prophets who had been sent to turn them back to God – a historical example of the pattern Jesus describes in the parable. [ref:Neh 9:26|Nehemiah 9:26]
Stephen accuses the people of having persecuted the prophets, just as their ancestors did – this confirms the historical pattern illustrated by the parable in Luke 20:10. [ref:Acts 7:52|Acts 7:52]
